intro.data: An Order names a customer by id; Customers each have an id. The pullback joins them on that shared key: it pairs an order ONLY with the customer whose id matches. Build the join that respects the key, then read off the customer — the matched pair gives the real customer. A loose join pairs the order with the wrong customer, so reading it gives a stranger. Pick the right join and projection.
intro.alchemy: An Ore carries a trait-mark; Reagents each bear a mark. The pullback pairs them on the shared mark: an ore ONLY with the reagent whose mark matches. Build the join that respects the mark, then read off the reagent. A loose join pairs the wrong reagent. Pick the right join and projection.
intro.spellcraft: A Rune bears a sigil; Wards each carry a sigil. The pullback pairs them on the shared sigil: a rune ONLY with the ward whose sigil matches. Build the join that respects the sigil, then read off the ward. A loose join pairs the wrong ward. Pick the right join and projection.
intro.abstract: Given f : A → C and g : B → C, the pullback P holds pairs with f(a) = g(b). Build the map into P that respects the key, then project to B. A pair with mismatched keys projects to the wrong element.

afterSuccess.data: You joined the order to the customer whose id matched, then read off that customer — the real one. That key-matching is exactly the pullback: it keeps only the pairs where the two arrows into the shared key agree (f∘p₁ = g∘p₂). The loose join paired a mismatched customer, so the projection returned a stranger.
afterSuccess.alchemy: You matched the ore to the reagent sharing its mark, then read it off — the real one. That is the pullback: only pairs whose arrows into the shared mark agree. The loose join matched the wrong reagent.
afterSuccess.spellcraft: You bound the rune to the ward sharing its sigil, then read it off — the real one. That is the pullback: only pairs whose arrows into the shared sigil agree. The loose bind matched the wrong ward.
afterSuccess.abstract: f∘p₁ = g∘p₂ held: the pullback keeps exactly the pairs whose keys agree, so projecting recovers the matched element. A mismatched pair violates the square and projects to the wrong element.

reveal.summary: The pullback of f : A → C and g : B → C is the object of matching pairs — those with f(a) = g(b) — with projections p₁, p₂ such that f∘p₁ = g∘p₂. It is a join on a key, and generalises the product (take C terminal).
reveal.programmerAnalogy: orders.join(customers).on(o => o.customerId === c.id) — an inner join on a key.
